name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea & STOP-Bang
cards: Three types of sleep-disordered breathing?
Obstructive apnea, central apnea, sleep-related hypoventilation.
Apnea definition?
Airflow drop of 90% or more lasting at least 10 seconds.
Hypopnea definition?
Slowed, shallow breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer.
Obstructive apnea: airflow and effort?
No airflow but continued respiratory effort.
Central apnea: airflow and effort?
No airflow and no respiratory effort.
Mixed apnea: airflow and effort?
No effort early in the event, then effort resumes.
Most common form of sleep-disordered breathing?
Obstructive sleep apnea.
Cause of obstructive sleep apnea?
Upper airway narrowing from excess soft tissue or structural abnormality.
Jaw risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea?
Micrognathia and retrognathia.
Tongue and throat risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea?
Macroglossia and enlarged tonsils.
Obstructive sleep apnea risk-factor neck circumference in men?
17 inches or more.
Obstructive sleep apnea risk-factor neck circumference in women?
16 inches or more.
Nighttime history clues for obstructive sleep apnea?
Loud habitual snoring, witnessed apnea, snorting or gasping awakenings.
Daytime symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea?
Sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, poor concentration or memory.
Blood pressure clue to obstructive sleep apnea?
Poorly controlled hypertension.
Gold-standard test for obstructive sleep apnea?
Polysomnogram, split-night or all-night.
Split-night polysomnogram sequence?
First 2 hours grade severity, then continuous positive airway pressure titration.
What can a home sleep test assess?
Only obstructive sleep apnea, not other sleep disorders.
Who needs a polysomnogram rather than a home sleep test?
Cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease, hypoventilation, stroke, long-term opioids.
Apnea-hypopnea index formula?
Apneas plus hypopneas divided by hours of sleep.
Obstructive sleep apnea diagnosis with symptoms?
5 or more obstructive events per hour plus a symptom.
Obstructive sleep apnea diagnosis regardless of symptoms?
15 or more obstructive events per hour.
Differential diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea?
Central sleep apnea, heart failure, nocturnal asthma, reflux, panic attacks, seizures.
STOP-Bang: S?
Snore loudly, heard through closed doors.
STOP-Bang: T?
Tired, fatigued, or sleepy in the daytime.
STOP-Bang: O?
Observed to stop breathing, choke, or gasp during sleep.
STOP-Bang: P?
Have or being treated for high blood pressure.
STOP-Bang: B?
Body mass index more than 35 kg/m2.
STOP-Bang: A?
Age older than 50.
STOP-Bang: N?
Neck (shirt collar) 16 inches / 40 cm or larger.
STOP-Bang: G?
Gender is male.
STOP-Bang low risk?
Yes to 0 to 2 questions.
STOP-Bang intermediate risk?
Yes to 3 to 4 questions.
STOP-Bang high risk?
Yes to 5 to 8 questions.
STOP-Bang high risk: 2 or more STOP yeses plus what?
Male gender, body mass index over 35, or neck 16 inches / 40 cm.
Main use of STOP-Bang?
Preoperative check of patients without known obstructive sleep apnea.

name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Treatment & Complications
cards: Stimulants for sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea?
Modafinil or armodafinil.
Modafinil side effects?
Headache, nervousness, dizziness, nausea, hypersensitivity reactions.
Conditions needing caution with modafinil?
Cardiovascular, hepatic, or psychiatric conditions.
Stimulant adjustment in elderly patients?
Use lower doses.
Nasal steroids in obstructive sleep apnea treat?
Nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis.
Most effective obstructive sleep apnea treatment?
Continuous positive airway pressure.
Autotitrating positive airway pressure suits whom?
Patients without significant comorbid conditions.
Positional therapy suits whom?
Patients whose events occur when supine.
Positional therapy device?
Sleep belt or shirt that keeps a lateral position.
When is an oral appliance not effective?
Severe obstructive sleep apnea or no teeth.
How does a nasal expiratory resistance device work?
Uses the patient's own breathing to create expiratory pressure.
Radiofrequency ablation candidate?
Mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea, intolerant of continuous positive airway pressure.
Palatal implant candidate?
Mild obstructive sleep apnea, intolerant of continuous positive airway pressure.
Surgical cure for obstructive sleep apnea?
Tracheostomy, which bypasses the obstruction.
Jaw surgery for obstructive sleep apnea?
Maxillomandibular advancement surgery.
Bariatric surgery in obstructive sleep apnea?
Weight loss that may help.
Risk modifications for obstructive sleep apnea?
Diet and exercise for weight loss; avoid alcohol and sedatives.
Referral for obstructive sleep apnea?
Refer to a sleep physician.
Driving accidents with untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
2.5 times more driving accidents.
Sudden cardiac death with untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
3 to 6 times the risk, at night.
Hypertension with untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
3 times the risk.
Morbidities of untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
Pulmonary hypertension, stroke, insulin resistance, arrhythmias, ischemic heart disease.
Reflux in untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
75% to 100% of patients.
Why does obstructive sleep apnea cause reflux?
Decreased intrathoracic pressure.
Pulmonary hypertension group for obstructive sleep apnea?
Group 3 pulmonary hypertension.
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease with obstructive sleep apnea?
2 to 3 times the prevalence.
Joint disease linked to obstructive sleep apnea?
Increased risk of gout.
Metabolic effects of obstructive sleep apnea?
Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, higher glucose and triglycerides.
Aortic risks of untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
Aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection.
Cardiovascular effects of untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
More sympathetic tone, bradycardia, blood pressure variability, arrhythmias.
Markers raised by untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
C-reactive protein, cortisol, and amyloid.
Hormones lowered by untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
Growth hormone and prolactin.
Immune effect of untreated obstructive sleep apnea?
More proinflammatory cytokines.
Obstructive sleep apnea mortality in the elderly?
Lower, because patients compensate.
Elderly obstructive sleep apnea symptoms that improve with continuous positive airway pressure?
Drowsiness and nocturia.

name: Central Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation
cards: Central sleep apnea mechanism?
The brainstem stops sending signals to breathe.
Central sleep apnea trigger?
Increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide.
Central sleep apnea breathing pattern?
Hyperventilation alternating with apnea.
Central sleep apnea risk factors?
Heart failure, stroke, opioids, hypoxia, high altitude, continuous positive airway pressure use.
Heart failure breathing pattern behind central sleep apnea?
Cheyne-Stokes breathing (hyperventilation alternating with apnea).
Cause of Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure?
Prolonged circulation delay from lung capillaries to carotid chemoreceptors.
Central sleep apnea symptoms?
Insomnia, frequent awakenings, nocturnal dyspnea, nonrestorative sleep.
Central sleep apnea diagnostic test?
Polysomnography; home testing is not sufficient.
Central sleep apnea polysomnogram finding?
Repeated apneas without thoracic-abdominal excursion.
Central sleep apnea from heart failure: first step?
Optimize heart failure therapy.
Central sleep apnea from opioids: first step?
Reduce the opioids.
Central sleep apnea at high altitude: first step?
Descend from altitude.
First device to try in central sleep apnea?
Continuous positive airway pressure.
Central sleep apnea device if continuous positive airway pressure fails?
Consider adaptive servo-ventilation.
How does adaptive servo-ventilation work?
Monitors breathing in real time and adjusts pressure.
Adaptive servo-ventilation caution group?
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Why is adaptive servo-ventilation risky with poor left ventricular function?
Reducing preload can decrease cardiac output.
Other name for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
Also called Pickwickian syndrome.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome definition?
Awake alveolar hypoventilation in obesity not explained by another condition.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome risk factors?
Central obesity, reduced lung function, weak inspiratory muscles, severe obstructive apnea.
Obesity hypoventilation patients with coexisting obstructive apnea?
90% of patients.
Late obesity hypoventilation syndrome presentation?
Hypoxemic hypercapnic respiratory failure and right heart failure.
Saturation that prompts obesity hypoventilation screening?
Awake 94% or less, or overnight low under 80%.
Facial sign prompting obesity hypoventilation screening?
Facial plethora (facial swelling, puffiness).
Lab clue prompting obesity hypoventilation screening?
Raised serum bicarbonate.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome body mass index criterion?
Body mass index over 30.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome awake carbon dioxide criterion?
Arterial carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg.
Why is obesity hypoventilation syndrome a diagnosis of exclusion?
Other causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation must be excluded.
Serum bicarbonate that calls for an arterial blood gas?
Serum bicarbonate above 27.
Gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring.
First-line obesity hypoventilation syndrome treatment?
Weight loss program plus positive airway pressure.
Device for obesity hypoventilation with obstructive apnea?
Continuous positive airway pressure.
Device for obesity hypoventilation with sleep-related hypoventilation?
BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure).
Effective second-line obesity hypoventilation syndrome therapy?
Tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation.
Leading cause of death in obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
Death from cardiovascular disease.
Main complications of obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.
